In a skip-dominated cell, another skip on edge 3 brings no learned transformation and further weakens the cell (row 17 strongly negative, while conv parents gain).
Filling an empty input-to-output edge adds a new path, whereas replacing an existing skip loses the residual shortcut (rows 87, 90 vs 86).
When edge 5 is empty, edge 4's conv carries most of the learned signal to the output, so swapping it for pooling hurts more (rows 39-40 vs 31, 33).
Pooling on an empty edge adds an extra aggregation path, while pooling in place of a conv loses learned capacity (rows 34, 36, 38 vs 31, 32, 37).

Deleting a conv on the edge into the output loses more than deleting a skip or pool there (rows 61-64, 68-70 vs 65-66).
If edge 4 is empty, removing edge 3 can leave the output with almost nothing feeding it, which collapses the network (row 83 vs 81-82).

I picked these 10 from the 100 experiments and from how NAS-Bench-201 cells work. Most rest on one or two very large effects; a couple of others (the edge 1 removal and the edge 4 pooling swap) rest on smaller, more uneven gaps, so they are the weakest picks.

- **Unblocking the output.** When edges 4 and 5 are both `none`, the output node receives only edge 3. Adding a conv on edge 3, 4 or 5 then makes the largest gains (rows 3, 4, 72, 90). Removing the last conv path makes the largest losses (rows 63, 64, 83).
- **Replacing `none` vs. replacing something useful.** An edit has a bigger effect when it fills an empty edge than when it replaces a conv or a skip. This shows in rows 71–80, 87 vs. 86, and 34/36 vs. 31–33.
- **Skip edge 3 in cells without convs.** Adding a skip on edge 3 hurts badly when the cell is all skips or all pooling (rows 17, 18). It helps when the cell is conv-based (rows 11–16).
- **The lone conv in a pooling cell.** In cells built from pooling, the first conv added makes a huge difference (row 30).
